title: Developer cookbook: quant kernel implementation and runtime integration
content:
Purpose:
This developer-facing cookbook condenses patterns, minimal working examples, test recipes, and runtime integration notes for shipping quantized kernels (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) into the serving runtime. Target audience: engineers who will author or onboard a kernel, QA engineers building CI tests, and SREs validating safety fallbacks.

High-level goals:
- Provide compact, copy-pasteable kernel stubs and registration examples for the runtime.
- Document KV-cache and scheduling constraints that commonly break when swapping precision paths.
- Give a reproducible CI/test matrix and smoke-tests for safe rollout.
- Surface common pitfalls and debug heuristics (determinism, numerical divergence, perf regression detection).

Scope and assumptions:
- This is not a spec for quant algorithms. It focuses on runtime integration: ABI, state transitions, KV-cache interactions, and fallback behavior.
- We assume kernel authors have a working optimized kernel (CUDA/ROCm) and will implement a thin adapter conforming to the runtime kernel API.

1) Kernel adapter checklist (minimal implementation)
- Exported symbol names: kernel_init_vX, kernel_forward_vX, kernel_shutdown_vX (match runtime version).
- Initialization must be idempotent and accept a serialized config blob (format v1: json-ish with keys: precision, profile_id, alignment, tile_shape).
- Must declare supported sequence length ranges and max KV memory usage via get_capabilities().
- Provide a deterministic pseudorandom seed path if using internal stochastic ops (top-k sampling helpers should be deterministic when provided same seed).
- Expose a small diagnostics API: query_counters(), last_error_code(), perf_counters(). These are polled by smoke tests.
- Dealloc must not block long-running inference threads; use deferred/free-queue pattern for device memory if necessary.

2) KV cache contract notes (things kernel authors must not break)
- Cache layout invariants: key/value tensors are sharded along the same batch axis as the runtime expects. Shard metadata (shard_id, offset, length) must be returned on init when the kernel requests dedicated kv shards.
- Replacement semantics: runtime expects append-only log-structured writes per request. Kernels may buffer writes but must flush (commit) before returning result if request.complete=true.
- Alignment: for int8/AWQ kernels that pack values, memory alignment must be 64B for NVLink DMA. Runtime will attempt zero-copy only when alignment constraints are satisfied; kernels must return alignment_hint in get_capabilities().
- Versioning: KVCACHE schema version must be returned. If kernel returns a mismatched schema, runtime will trigger a graceful fallback to reference kernel.

3) Scheduling and batching constraints
- Latency SLOs: kernels should provide an SLO hint: base_latency_ms@1, p95_latency_ms@1, throughput_qps@N. Use microbench harness (see testing) to generate these numbers.
- Batching safety: if kernel performs aggressive batching internal to the device, it must provide max_internal_batch_size and a preemptibility flag. If preemptible=false, runtime will avoid interleaving low-priority requests.
- Preemption contract: kernel preemption must drain partially executed KV states or provide a recover_point that the runtime can use to resume. If not implemented, scheduler will forestall preemption for that kernel type.

4) Fallback & compatibility behaviors (recommended)
- Soft-fallback: when kernel init fails under certain conditions (unsupported seq len, insufficient memory), runtime will attempt a soft-fallback to a compatible kernel. Kernel should surface a canonical compatibility string like "gptq-1.0-compatible-with:int8-ref" for matching.
- Hard-fallback: runtime may evict the kernel completely from the pool for downstream requests if the kernel reports deterministic incorrectness on conformance tests. Kernel author must supply a fix branch and a conformance vector to validate a patch.

5) Test matrix (CI) and smoke tests (copyable)
- Local microbench harness (docker image: rw/inference-quant-harness:ci): runs per-precision tests. Steps: build kernel artifact -> load into harness -> run default-config microbench -> run kv-fuzz tests -> run deterministic-seed tests.
- Required CI checks: build (linux-cuda, linux-rocm), conformance (numerical tolerance table), perf-regression (compare baseline tokens/sec with +/-10% threshold), kv-consistency (write/read roundtrip), memory-leak (1000 request soak).
- Example smoke test script (bash pseudocode):
  # load kernel into runtime test node
  runtest --load ./libmyquant.so --profile profile.json 
  runtest --call "infer --prompt 'hello' --seq-len 128 --seed 42" > out1.json
  runtest --call "infer --prompt 'hello' --seq-len 128 --seed 42" > out2.json
  diff out1.json out2.json || exit 1  # determinism check
  runtest --kv-fuzz --iterations 1000 || exit 1

Acceptance criteria for merge to main branch:
- All CI checks green on linux-cuda, linux-rocm.
- No new numerical regression beyond listed tolerances for the model family.
- KV roundtrip passes on both small- and large-shard configs.

6) Diagnostics and perf counters to expose (runtime polls these)
- tokens_emitted, avg_ms_per_token, kv_reads, kv_writes, kv_cache_hits, internal_reductions, warp_occupancy_estimate, last_error_code (string), last_warning_tags (list).
- Add a compact health endpoint that returns JSON with above counters; tests poll this endpoint during soak tests.

7) Example kernel stub (pseudo-C++ outline)
- The content below is intentionally high-level and should be copied into the kernel repo as the initial adapter:

  // export symbols as C ABI
  extern "C" int kernel_init_v1(const char* json_config, char* out_capabilities, int out_len);
  extern "C" int kernel_forward_v1(const RequestBatch* batch, ResponseBatch* out);
  extern "C" void kernel_shutdown_v1();

  // init should parse config and set alignment/seq-len limits
  int kernel_init_v1(const char* json_config, char* out_capabilities, int out_len) {
    // parse, allocate gpu buffers pinned host buffers for zero-copy RN, return capabilities blob
  }

8) Rollout plan (canary -> regional -> global)
- Canary: single-region, 5% of traffic, disabled for high-priority customers. Enable KV persistence toggled off. Observe perf counters for 24h.
- Regional ramp: increment traffic to 25% after 72h if no perf regressions and KV error rate < 0.1%.
- Global: 100% after A/B pass comparing token quality metrics.

9) Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Non-determinism due to uninitialized memory: always zero-initialize device scratch regions.
- Silent precision drift: add deterministic unit tests with reference fp32 outputs and tolerances per-layer.
- KV-density surprises: kernels that pack values into 4-bit lanes can blow expected kv sizes; add explicit kv_size_estimate() that runtime uses to accept/deny placement.

10) Open questions / TODOs:
- Should the runtime mandate a single canonical health schema for all kernels (proposal: yes; v1 draft in linked artifacts)?
- How to version capabilities blob to allow out-of-band extension without breaking older runtime nodes? (design options: semantic-versioned key/value pairs vs TLV)
- Investigate adding a "simulated-oom" hook in CI to validate graceful fallback behavior under memory pressure.

References and quick links:
- Confluence: Quant Kernel Specs (linked above)
- GitHub: quant-kernels repo module naming conventions
- Jira: test tickets and rollout checklist

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- This is intended as a living doc—please add short recipes you used while onboarding kernels (e.g., profiling knobs that mattered for H100 vs MI250).
- If you add a code snippet in the repo, copy the CI steps here with exact docker image tags so others can reproduce.

Unresolved items (placeholders):
